From the statement released (and their link to their original objection) by the EFF it seems pretty clear that it wasn't the DRM capabilities for content producers of EME that the EFF was disappointed with but rather that large corporations within the W3C were advocating for retaining proprietary control at the web standard level and not allow "research and modifications, that required circumvention of DRM". This benefits no-one, not even the content producers and holders (such as Netflix), except the people responsible for creating the DRM technologies that would be compatible within this EME framework. An example of this is the Adobe Content Decryption Module found within Mozilla's Firefox. The fucking absurdity that got accepted in the EME proposal made by W3C is what forces Firefox to run this shit in an extra fucking sandbox to secure the user from whatever the fuck this plugin is doing. It's not in Netflix's best interests to develop all this proprietary software (since I doubt they'd have an interest in reselling whatever technology they develop) or have to pay for some closed source shit. This guy on Ars Technica seems to hit the nail on the head with regards to what the issue with EME is. This seems like a step backward rather than a step forward. Netflix already has protection rights over their content (which they care about 100x more than anything else) so again, this isn't in their interest but rather the interest of the people creating the technologies within EME.

While I haven't personally used anything that relies on EME (which is where the fuss is about) I have actually needed to host encrypted videos where the underlying technology was built using MSE which is related to EME. This was in a desire to watch copyrighted movies with my friends. Because my upload speed is too shit to stream high-bitrate content to several people I had to rely on an external host to serve the video files. This is where I purchased a cheap VPS. The problem though is that most cheap VPSes are pretty stingy as to what is running or being hosted on their servers. If you're using a lot of resources (like high-bitrate video streaming to several people definitely does) then they'll try to look for any reason to shut you down. If I had clear unencrypted video then the VPS provider would have no problems viewing the original video files themselves (and they'd shut me down for a clear copyright violation). This is where I needed to find some solution to play synchronized encrypted video (the rationale being that they'd have much less reason to cancel my service if they can't see the video file being hosted). To no surprise, no ready made solution for synchronized encrypted video exists. There was a good number of steps necessary to create this (which are irrelevant to this post) but what's relevant to this post was how the content was going to be encrypted. After spending a few days doing on and off research I found out that as an end-user/somebody who just wants to host encrypted content there was only Apple's HLS and MPEG-DASH. I settled with Apple's HLS (for practical reasons) but neither are 100% free and open-source. While Apple's HLS doesn't really have any information regarding licensing, their solution can only currently support MPEG-2 TS containers which is owned by MPEG-LA and charges $$$ for commercial uses. MPEG-DASH is also patented by MPEG-LA so you don't really have any choice here either.
